title: When the Guard Adds Nothing: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair (G‑V‑R) for LLM‑Produced Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (n=300 tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) pipeline increases the probability that an LLM‑produced vendor CLI configuration passes a conservative deterministic validator, compared to direct LLM generation. Using a curated multi‑intent 300‑task manifest, a frozen deterministic validator encoding syntactic, interface‑assignment, basic reachability and destructive‑pattern checks, and the declared model snapshot gpt-5-mini, every shared initial candidate passed the validator (baseline = 300/300; guarded = 300/300; n11=300, n10=n01=n00=0). The paired difference is 0.00 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10k resamples, seed = 1729). Because no initial failures occurred the preregistered guarded single‑repair policy was never invoked. We publish all raw outputs, provider traces, deterministic validator traces, the task manifest, the preregistration, and analysis artifacts (hash‑signed) to support reproducible follow‑ups that vary task hardness, validator scope, and model family.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into vendor CLI configuration fragments for NetOps automation. Safety and operational trust require deterministic safeguards (parsers, validators, guarded repairs) and rigorous, evidence‑anchored measurement of whether such safeguards materially improve operational correctness. We preregistered the paired study reported here (study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e; preregistration SHA‑256 = a85d66d4c6ce2275e2d8c820f96c610532dbb5452bebb3fe108848f9dc38cdf6) to answer one focused question: to what extent does a deterministic, bounded generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) pipeline increase the probability that an LLM‑produced vendor CLI configuration passes a conservative deterministic validator, compared to direct LLM generation? The design intentionally fixes a single shared initial generation per task and compares baseline = validator(initial) to guarded = validator(initial) OR validator(repair) with at most one automatic repair call. This shared‑initial design isolates the additional value of the repair stage for a given initial candidate by eliminating between‑generation variability; a direct consequence (predeclared in the preregistration) is that if the initial candidate passes for all tasks the repair branch is unexercised. Our run archived every raw response, provider trace, validator trace, and analysis artifact with canonical hashes to enable independent verification (see Table 2 artifact list and hashes).
sections.related_work: Prior work on LLM‑driven intent→configuration and intent‑based networking (Nguyen et al., 2024; Chakraborty et al., 2024; Mondal et al., 2025) demonstrates methods to synthesize vendor CLI from natural intent and to integrate verification. Deterministic/formal verification for network control (Bagpipe/SMT approaches, Weitz et al.) motivates validator design choices that favor auditable, reproducible checks. Recent self‑correction and tool‑assisted refinement literature (INTERACSPARQL, LATCH, tool‑augmented self‑refinement) establishes architectures like G‑V‑R and bounded repair loops; these motivate our single‑repair bounded policy. Benchmarks for LLM network tasks (NetLLMBench, intent‑to‑configuration efforts) shaped our task manifest. All cited records referenced in this manuscript are verified and listed in the Cited Record Ids field (artifact‑anchored references).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The preregistered plan defines a paired binary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline across n=300 task pairs. The preregistration freezes inclusion/exclusion rules, retry policy, contamination detection, the shared‑initial design (one initial generation per task shared by both arms), the guarded single‑repair policy (at most one deterministic repair call per task), and the exact analysis tests (exact McNemar two‑sided test plus paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI, 10k resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistration artifact and hash appear in the Evidence Bundle.

Task manifest. We used a curated 300‑task manifest of operator intents limited to vendor CLI fragments and annotated with per‑task initial state, required safe‑sequence constraints, and difficulty metadata. The canonical manifest is archived at execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3). Each manifest entry encodes intent text, initial network state, required safe command sequences, and explicit per‑task workflow policies (examples: "must_be_down_for_fields", "make_before_break"). The manifest is the authoritative provenance object for task content and per‑task annotations.

Validator. Scoring used a conservative deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, version 5.0). The validator deterministically parses and canonicalizes vendor CLI text, enforces syntactic correctness, checks per‑task workflow invariants (e.g., required shutdown before MTU or VLAN change, minimum active interface constraints), detects destructive global patterns (egress uplink disable, mass shutdown), and emits structured validator traces (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, final_state). Validator traces for every episode are archived under execution/scoring/*.json (example execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json; SHA‑256 = 1c3cbbeb30cb9d0...). The validator intentionally omits nondeterministic runtime/emulation checks so scoring remains fully reproducible and deterministic.

Model, prompt, and execution contract. The declared generator snapshot was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Execution used a shared initial generation per task (one provider call per task) to remove generator sampling variance from the primary estimand; the guarded arm could only change the outcome by invoking the single repair call when the shared initial candidate failed. The preregistered maximum_model_calls = 600; the run used 300 model calls (shared initial only). All provider traces and raw responses are archived under execution/provider_calls/* and execution/responses/*; the full hash manifest is in the execution manifest.

Sampling, scoring, and analysis. For each task the pipeline: (1) produced one shared initial candidate using the declared prompt and model; (2) computed baseline outcome = validator(initial); (3) computed guarded outcome = validator(initial) OR (if initial failed) validator(repair) after one automatic repair attempt; and (4) recorded per‑episode validator traces. The primary test is the exact two‑sided McNemar on paired binary outcomes; we also compute a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap seed=1729). Contamination detection (exact/fuzzy matches to public sources and high‑entropy token heuristics) and missingness policies were executed as preregistered; flags and counts are archived in analysis/contamination_summary.csv and analysis/missingness_summary.csv. Analysis code, inputs, and outputs are archived (analysis/*) and hash‑signed.

sections.discussion:
Interpreting a ceiling outcome. The observed ceiling (300/300 initial validator passes) means that under the declared model snapshot, prompt, and curated manifest, the single initial draw already satisfied the conservative deterministic validator for every task. Under our shared‑initial design the guarded arm could only change an outcome if the shared initial candidate failed; therefore the guarded repair branch could not be exercised. This is a predeclared design tradeoff: fixing the initial candidate isolates repair utility per candidate at the cost of sensitivity to ceiling effects. The preregistration recorded this tradeoff and specified sensitivity analyses and alternative designs for future runs.

Operational implication. The null measured benefit does not imply repairs are never useful; it identifies an operational regime where a carefully prompted generator produced validator‑passing outputs across the curated task set. In deployments where generator prompt/model produce high initial pass rates, bounded repair orchestration introduces additional cost (extra model calls, orchestration complexity) without measured validator gains. Conversely, in harder or adversarial task regimes — or with other model snapshots — repair may be essential. The archived artifacts enable exact replication and controlled perturbations (harder manifest slices, independent per‑arm draws, iterative repairs, or adding dynamic emulation checks) to explore such regimes.

Design choices and alternatives. The shared‑initial design was chosen to answer a narrowly interpretable estimand: the marginal value of repair for a fixed initial candidate. An alternative design (independent initial draws per arm or multiple independent generator draws per task) estimates expected population gains from repair under generator stochasticity but requires larger budgets and more complex paired analyses. Our artifact bundle contains the manifest, scoring code, and execution scripts to rerun either design.

Reproducibility and artifact guidance. All execution artifacts (raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, task manifest, model_configuration.json, transformation manifest, analysis inputs and outputs) are archived with canonical SHA‑256 hashes in the execution manifest and Table 2. Example artifact paths: execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a7...), execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = 1acce925...), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA‑256 = a39fd338...). The deterministic validator traces include normalized configurations and validator decisions per episode to enable external auditors to re‑run scoring without nondeterministic components. The run used no undisclosed technical restarts outside the preregistered retry policy and recorded all provider call traces (execution/provider_calls/*).

Threats to validity (expanded). Internal: shared initial candidate design reduces generator variance but produces ceiling vulnerability; the single model snapshot and prompt create model‑selection risk. Construct: the deterministic validator enforces important syntactic and workflow invariants but omits dynamic routing/emulation checks—validator passes are necessary but not sufficient for runtime safety. External: single model snapshot (gpt‑5‑mini), single manifest, and curated task selection limit broad generalization. Conclusion validity: zero discordant pairs collapse inferential variability; the CI degeneracy reflects that fact and is an honest statistical statement under the preregistered estimand. We enumerate these threats in the limitations and provide the full artifact set for researchers to execute alternative designs that trade off variance and bias differently.

Reviewer‑requested clarifications addressed. Per peer review we (1) explicitly state the shared‑initial design consequence: both arms used the identical initial generation per task, so the guarded arm could only affect outcomes when that shared initial failed (this sentence is in Methods and highlighted in Results), and (2) provide the canonical task manifest path and its SHA‑256 (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3). The reviewer requested an in‑manuscript numeric per‑vendor count; the archived manifest encodes per‑task adapter/vendor labels programmatically but the manifest listing (artifact) is the authoritative source. The artifact path and hash are provided for immediate audit; we do not invent per‑vendor counts that are not explicitly summarized in the archived manifest.
sections.conclusion: We ran a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment to quantify whether a bounded G‑V‑R pipeline improves the validator pass probability over direct LLM generation for a curated set of 300 NetOps intent tasks. Under the declared generator/prompt/model and a conservative deterministic validator every shared initial candidate passed (300/300), so the guarded single‑repair policy was never invoked and produced no measurable improvement (paired difference = 0.00; McNemar p = 1.00; 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]). The outcome is a concrete, reproducible datum: in this operational regime the extra orchestration cost of adding a bounded repair step produced no validator benefit. All raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, task manifest, preregistration, and analysis artifacts are published and hash‑signed to enable alternative designs (harder tasks, other model snapshots, independent draws, richer validators) where G‑V‑R may show value.

limitations: Single model snapshot (gpt-5-mini) evaluated — results do not generalize to other models or model versions.

Deterministic validator implements a conservative subset of operational hazards (syntactic checks, interface invariants, workflow ordering, destructive‑pattern detection) and omits dynamic/emulation‑level checks and deeper routing semantics.

Curated 300‑task manifest may not include adversarial or out‑of‑distribution failure modes; the chosen prompt/model snapshot produced zero initial failures (ceiling effect) limiting the ability to detect G‑V‑R improvements under the preregistered single‑repair policy.
Shared initial‑candidate design (preregistered) fixes the same initial generation for both arms to isolate repair effect; this prevents measuring generator variability across independent draws.
Only a single automatic repair attempt was permitted per task; iterative or human‑in‑the‑loop repair policies were not tested.
Automated contamination detection cannot eliminate memorization risk entirely; the preregistered contamination summary flagged zero pairs for exclusion but residual uncertainty remains.
